title: Iran Wants Up to $2 Million Per Tanker to Cross Hormuz. India Sends a Fifth of Its Oil Through That Strait.
excerpt: Tehran has drafted legislation to charge transit fees in rials, barter, or even cryptocurrency. The US has warned Oman not to cooperate. India, Japan, and every refiner in Asia is watching.
body:
Before the war began on February 28, approximately 21 million barrels of oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz every day. One-fifth of the world's crude. One-third of its liquefied natural gas. The narrow channel between Iran and Oman was the most important chokepoint in global energy — and everyone treated it as a given.

That assumption is now dead.

On Monday, Iran's ambassador to Moscow, Kazem Jalali, told the Russian newspaper Izvestia that the Strait of Hormuz would reopen — but under new conditions. "Of course, this strait will be open, but with new conditions to be determined by the Iranian and Omani authorities," Jalali said. "We understand that Iran and Oman provide certain services related to this strait. And fees will be charged for those services."

## What the Fees Look Like

Iran has already moved beyond rhetoric. The country's parliament has approved a bill authorising transit fees for oil tankers passing through Hormuz, with charges estimated between $150,000 and $2 million per voyage, according to Fars News Agency. Payments could be made in Iranian rials, through barter arrangements, or — in what may be the most eyebrow-raising clause — in cryptocurrency, including Bitcoin. A separate $1-per-barrel digital asset fee has also been floated.

Tehran frames the toll as compensation for "security services" and environmental restoration. Arman Khorsand, head of Iran's International Affairs and Environmental Conventions Center, said the charges are grounded in the principle of "innocent passage" under international maritime law, which allows coastal states to collect fees for services rendered and environmental damage suffered. Iran has drafted the Strait of Hormuz Environmental Service Charge Regulation to formalise the move.

## Why This Matters for India

India imported roughly 4.5 million barrels of oil per day before the war, with about 60 percent of that flowing through the Strait of Hormuz. Even as Indian refiners have scrambled to diversify — buying more from Venezuela, Brazil, Angola, and Nigeria — any toll regime on Hormuz would reshape the economics of India's oil imports for years.

At the lower end of Iran's proposed fee schedule, $150,000 per tanker, the cost across India's annual tanker traffic through Hormuz would run into hundreds of millions of dollars. At the upper end, $2 million per very large crude carrier, the bill would be significantly higher. That cost would ultimately land on Indian consumers — at petrol pumps, in LPG cylinder prices, and in the cost of every manufactured good that depends on petroleum.

The geopolitical implications are equally serious. Iran has not ratified the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which explicitly prohibits charges on vessels exercising the right of transit passage through international straits. Legal scholars warn that if Iran successfully imposes a toll on Hormuz, it could set a precedent for other strategic chokepoints — the Strait of Malacca, the Suez Canal approach, the Bab el-Mandeb.

## The American and Omani Response

The United States has pushed back hard. In late May, Washington warned Oman — which shares sovereignty over the strait — not to cooperate with any Iranian toll scheme. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Oman's ambassador had told him there were no plans to impose such tolls. Japan, which sourced about 95 percent of its oil from the Middle East before the war, said it did not pay any fee when a Japan-linked tanker passed through Hormuz in May.

But Iran's bargaining position is stronger than it appears. Tehran has already demonstrated that it can effectively close the strait — oil and LNG flows remain severely constrained, even as a few tankers have slipped through recently. The Hormuz blockade, combined with the U.S. counter-blockade of Iranian ports, has created the world's largest supply crisis. OPEC+ production has collapsed from 42.77 million barrels per day in February to 33.19 million in April, according to OPEC figures.

## What Happens Next

JPMorgan predicts Hormuz will reopen in June and expects Brent crude to remain near $100 per barrel for most of the year. If the strait stays closed, each additional month could add $5 to $15 per barrel to oil price forecasts, with inventories declining and fuel margins already at extraordinary levels — gasoline refining margins around $35 a barrel, diesel near $60.

For India, the question is not just whether Hormuz reopens, but on what terms. A strait that comes with a toll is a different strait. And a toll denominated in rials or cryptocurrency, rather than dollars, would signal a fundamental shift in the architecture of global energy trade — one that New Delhi is almost certainly not prepared for.

As Capital Economics commodities economist Hamad Hussain told the Wall Street Journal: "The genie is out of the bottle given that the longstanding threat of Iran effectively closing the strait has now materialised." The genie, it seems, now wants to be paid.
